title: Srebrenica Under Bombardment: Morillon's Promise
sources: ICTY Karadzic Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T), Srebrenica 1993 findings
content:
By early 1993, the eastern Bosnian enclave of Srebrenica had become a symbol of the war's cruelty. Tens of thousands of Bosniak civilians and displaced persons were crowded into the small town and its surrounding villages, having fled or been expelled from communities across the Drina Valley during the ethnic cleansing campaigns of 1992. The enclave was surrounded on all sides by forces of the Vojska Republike Srpske, cut off from meaningful resupply, and subject to persistent shelling.

The VRS offensive against the Srebrenica pocket intensified sharply in the early months of 1993. Bosnian Serb forces under the Drina Corps systematically contracted the enclave's perimeter, seizing outlying villages and directing artillery and mortar fire into areas dense with civilians. The shelling was not incidental to military operations against ARBiH defenders — it was directed at the population itself. Shells struck the town center, its makeshift hospital, and areas where displaced persons had gathered in the open. Humanitarian conditions were catastrophic: food supplies were exhausted, medical care was virtually nonexistent, and winter compounded the suffering of a population already at the edge of survival.

The ICTY Karadžić Trial Judgment (IT-95-5/18-T) examined the 1993 Srebrenica offensive extensively, finding that the campaign of shelling and territorial compression was part of a broader pattern of conduct aimed at making life unbearable for the Bosniak population of eastern Bosnia. The evidence established that the Bosnian Serb political and military leadership was informed of conditions in the enclave and continued to authorize operations that worsened them.

It was in this context that General Philippe Morillon, commander of UNPROFOR in Bosnia-Herzegovina, made his dramatic visit to Srebrenica in March 1993. Morillon entered the enclave to assess conditions and found himself confronted by desperate civilians who physically blocked his departure, pleading for protection. On 12 March, standing before the crowd, Morillon declared that the town was under the protection of the United Nations and that he would never abandon them. The promise was personal and spontaneous — it carried no formal mandate from the Security Council, no commitment of military resources, and no mechanism for enforcement.

Yet Morillon's pledge had immediate political consequences. International media coverage of the enclave's plight intensified, and pressure mounted on the Security Council to act. Within weeks, the Council adopted Resolution 819 on 16 April 1993, declaring Srebrenica a "safe area" — the first use of that designation in the Bosnian conflict. The resolution demanded that all parties treat the enclave as free from armed attack and from any hostile act. A ceasefire was brokered, and a limited UNPROFOR presence — a limited UNPROFOR contingent — was deployed into the pocket.

The arrangement satisfied no one. The ARBiH garrison was required to disarm under the demilitarization agreement negotiated by General Philippe Morillon and UNPROFOR commanders, surrendering weapons to UNPROFOR custody. Bosniak leadership viewed this as stripping the enclave's defenders while providing no credible guarantee of security in return. The VRS, for its part, regarded the safe area declaration as an obstacle to the completion of its military objectives in the Drina Valley, though it accepted the ceasefire as a temporary expedient. UNPROFOR's presence was too small to defend the enclave and too lightly armed to deter a serious assault.

What Morillon's promise and Resolution 819 created was not safety but an intermediate condition — a pause in the enclave's agony that deferred rather than resolved the fundamental question of whether the international community would use force to protect civilians. That question would not be answered for another two years.
